result: The authors obtained cryo-EM structures of Y. lipolytica complex I in both the deactive form (4.3 Å resolution, 124,626 particles, 42 subunits, 7515 residues, 88% complete) and during steady-state turnover (4.5 Å resolution). The deactive structure agrees well with the previous X-ray structure (r.m.s.d. 1.768 Å) but is significantly more complete. The preparation was homogeneous with one major class, and ~30% of particles contained the substoichiometric ST1 subunit.
evaluation: Claims C5, C6, C29-C34, C36-C38 provide comprehensive structural data including resolution, particle numbers, model completeness, and comparison with prior structures. The technical details are internally consistent and supported by figures showing data quality metrics (Figures 1-3, Table 1). The homogeneity claim (C36) is supported by observation of a single major class, contrasting with mammalian complex I heterogeneity.

result: The overall structure of the fourteen central subunits is conserved across species. Species-specific features include: the 49 kDa subunit has a long N-terminal extension in mammalian and Y. lipolytica complex I; the 30 kDa subunit N-terminal extension reaches toward ST1 in Y. lipolytica; ND3 C-terminal extension contacts NUFM; TMH4 of ND6 was reassigned and differs in position between yeast and mammalian complex I; absence of ND2 TMH1-3 in mammals creates an indentation not present in yeast.
evaluation: Claims C39-C45 describe structural features of central subunits with specific comparisons between species. These observations are directly supported by the cryo-EM density maps and structural comparisons shown in Figures 6-7. The reassignment of ND6 TMH4 (C43) represents a correction to previous work based on improved resolution.

result: All 28 expected accessory subunits of Y. lipolytica complex I were identified, plus a new single-transmembrane helix subunit (X). Eighteen accessory subunits showed 59-98% side chain density. NESM and NUZM have extra domains; NUFM N-terminal extension interacts with ND3 C-terminal extension. NI2M, NB5M, and NIDM are smaller in Y. lipolytica than mammals. Three mammalian subunits (NDUFA10, NDUFV3, NDUFB1) are absent, consistent with genomic data. N7BM shares extensive interface with ST1, which also contacts NUZM and the 30 kDa subunit.
evaluation: Claims C46-C59 provide detailed characterization of accessory subunits supported by density maps (Figure 8, Table 2). The identification of a new subunit (C47) and assignment of NUXM (C56-C57) are based on density, secondary structure prediction, and biochemical data. The correlation between absent density and genomic absence (C53-C54) provides independent validation.

result: Four lipid molecules were identified in the membrane arm. An unassigned prominent density in ND1 near the PSST/49 kDa interface contacts conserved arginines (Arg36ND1, Arg297ND1) and is near the proposed ubiquinone access pathway. The density is too bulky for ubiquinone and likely represents a negatively charged lipid head group. Mass spectrometry detected >60 lipids per complex I. The density persists during turnover and may act as a 'hydrophobic valve' allowing ubiquinone access while excluding hydrophilic compounds.
evaluation: Claims C60-C74 describe an intriguing unassigned density with functional speculation. While the density is clearly observed (C61-C62, Figure 9) and mass spectrometry confirms abundant lipids (C68), the assignment as a lipid head group (C67) is speculative. The 'hydrophobic valve' hypothesis (C73-C74) is creative but lacks direct experimental support. Higher resolution or additional experiments would be needed to definitively assign this density.

result: In the deactive Y. lipolytica structure, the ubiquinone binding site shows limited disorder compared to mammalian complex I. Only residues 35-48 of the ND3 TMH1-2 loop are disordered. Continuous density was observed for the 49 kDa β1-β2 loop and ND1 TMH5-6 loop (disordered in bovine). The NUEM C-terminal domain was modeled with side chains (disordered in mammalian 39 kDa subunit). The region was modeled as poly-alanine due to flexibility.
evaluation: Claims C75-C83 describe the ubiquinone binding region in the deactive state with explicit comparisons to mammalian structures. The observations are directly supported by density maps (Figure 10) and represent a key difference from the 'unfolded Q site model' proposed for mammalian complex I. The limited disorder in Y. lipolytica is consistent with its lower energy barrier for A/D transition (discussed later).

result: To capture complex I during steady-state turnover, the authors developed an artificial respiratory chain using decylubiquinone (DBQ) and ubiquinol oxidase from Vitreoscilla at 18°C. The oxidase recycled ubiquinone, with complex I being rate-limiting. Steady-state conditions were sustained for >1 minute while grid freezing took 20-30 seconds.
evaluation: Claims C84-C88 describe the experimental strategy for capturing turnover. The approach is well-justified (C84-C85) and validated by oxygen consumption measurements showing complex I is rate-limiting (C86, Figure 11). The timing is appropriate for capturing steady-state (C87-C88). This represents a technically sophisticated solution to a challenging experimental problem.

result: Comparison of deactive and turnover structures shows no overall conformational changes. Large-scale rearrangements such as arm movements or piston-like motion of the lateral helix can be excluded.
evaluation: Claims C89-C91 report the absence of large conformational changes, directly supported by structural overlay (Figure 12). This negative result is important as it rules out previously proposed mechanisms (C90-C91 cite Böttcher et al. 2002; Hunte et al. 2010; Baradaran et al. 2013). The conclusion is well-supported by the structural data.

result: Under turnover conditions, NADH binds to the 51 kDa subunit with the pyridine ring stacking against FMN for hydride transfer. The adenine ring π-stacks with Phe92, Phe100, and Phe231. Lys228 forms a salt bridge with pyrophosphate and Ser325 hydrogen bonds to ribose. A slight movement of the glycine-rich loop (Gly88-Gly91) accommodates substrate binding.
evaluation: Claims C92-C97 describe NADH binding with specific molecular interactions supported by density (Figure 13A) and agreement with bacterial complex I structure (Berrisford and Sazanov, 2009). The detailed interactions are consistent with the resolution and represent expected substrate binding for this enzyme.

result: During turnover, the 49 kDa β1-β2 loop reorganizes, widening the cavity. A clear ubiquinone head group density appears between the 49 kDa β1-β2 loop and PSST α2 helix, ~12 Å from cluster N2. This position matches a ubiquinone-antagonistic inhibitor site from X-ray crystallography and differs from the bacterial T. thermophilus site (~2 Å closer to N2). Mutagenesis data support that both sites exist in mitochondrial enzyme and alternate during catalysis.
evaluation: Claims C98-C105 describe the key finding of ubiquinone binding during turnover. The density is clearly observed (C99, Figure 13B-C), matches inhibitor binding (C100, Figure 13D), and differs from bacterial structure (C102-C103, Figure 14A). The inference that both sites alternate (C105) is supported by mutagenesis data (C104, Tocilescu et al. 2010). This is the central mechanistic finding of the paper.

result: The authors' data address two competing models for the A/D transition. The 'unfolded Q site model' (Blaza et al. 2018) proposed that inhibitor prevented unfolding in Y. lipolytica, but this is excluded since no inhibitor was present in the current structure. Unfolding was not observed in Y. lipolytica to the extent seen in mammals. Species-dependent disorder may reflect different energy barriers for A/D transition. The NDUFA5/NDUFA10 interface effect in mouse cannot apply to Y. lipolytica which lacks NDUFA10.
evaluation: Claims C106-C116 critically evaluate competing models. The exclusion of the inhibitor hypothesis (C111-C112) is definitive based on the current data (C112). The observation of limited unfolding (C113) contradicts predictions of the 'unfolded Q site model'. The correlation with energy barriers (C114) is speculative but reasonable. The NDUFA10 argument (C115-C116) is logically sound.

result: The data provide direct evidence for a second ubiquinone binding site (P-state) that dominates during steady-state turnover. The only notable difference from D-form is β1-β2 loop reorganization. The findings support an integrated functional model where D-form represents the P-state of the catalytic cycle. The 12 Å distance is within electron transfer range but other parameters (reorganization energy, packing density) likely slow transfer sufficiently for the proposed mechanism. The E-state is predicted to be short-lived under uncoupled conditions.
evaluation: Claims C119-C131 present the authors' mechanistic interpretation. The observation of a second binding site (C119-C120) is well-supported by data (C121-C122, Figure 13). However, the mechanistic model (C124-C131) involves substantial speculation. The distance argument (C127-C130) acknowledges that 12 Å is within electron transfer range but invokes unmeasured parameters to explain impaired reduction. The prediction about E-state lifetime (C131) is untested. The model is plausible but requires additional experimental validation.

result: The proposed catalytic mechanism involves: (1) rapid ubiquinone reduction at E-site by cluster N2; (2) unstable semiquinone triggers E→P conversion creating alternate binding site; (3) stabilization of charged intermediates drives electrostatic power stroke transmitted through protonable residues to membrane arm; (4) protonation produces neutral semiquinone allowing return to E-state; (5) second electron transfer triggers another power stroke via ubiquinol anion stabilization.
evaluation: Claims C132-C137 describe a detailed mechanistic model (Figure 14B-C). While the model is internally consistent and integrates the structural observations, it remains largely speculative. C132 cites kinetic data (Krishnamoorthy and Hinkle, 1988) but C133-C137 are mechanistic proposals without direct experimental support in this study. The model makes testable predictions but requires validation through additional experiments (mutagenesis, kinetics, spectroscopy).

result: The cryo-EM structure under turnover conditions corroborates predictions of the two-state stabilization change mechanism and provides strong support for the integrated functional model describing energy conversion and regulation in complex I.
evaluation: Claims C138-C139 are summary statements. The structure does provide evidence for key predictions: two ubiquinone binding sites (C119-C120), limited conformational changes (C121-C122), and link between A/D transition and catalytic cycle (C123). However, 'strong support' may overstate the case given the speculative elements in the mechanistic model (C124-C137). The structural data are solid but mechanistic validation is incomplete.

result: The purified Y. lipolytica complex I preparation had activity of 1.8 µmol⁻¹mg⁻¹min⁻¹ under standard conditions (60 µM DBQ, no lipid/detergent), increasing to 5.9 µmol⁻¹mg⁻¹min⁻¹ upon lipid reactivation, and 13.9 µmol⁻¹mg⁻¹min⁻¹ under bovine assay conditions (200 µM DBQ, 0.15% asolectin, 0.15% CHAPS).
evaluation: Claims C140-C142 report enzyme activity measurements that validate the preparation quality. The activities are reasonable for complex I and the lipid-dependent activation (C141) is expected. These data confirm the enzyme is functional, which is essential for interpreting the turnover structure.
